text: Picture the stress in the skin as lines of force, flowing around a hole. Around a round hole, they bend smoothly, and the load is shared. But at a sharp corner, they have to squeeze around a tight turn. The stress piles up right at the tip, several times higher than in the rest of the skin. Engineers call this a stress concentration. And a tiny crack at a corner is an even sharper corner, so once it starts, it grows faster and faster. The Comet's skin was thin, and its openings had tight, almost square corners. Windows, hatches, and a small window in the roof for a navigation antenna. And many rivet holes were punched, not drilled, leaving tiny flaws right where the stress was highest.
